Reading the flames

The profiler draws the same recording two ways. In one, left to right is time; in the other, it isn't. Here's how to read each, and where a slow function really spends its time.

Diagram Mechanism Check your understanding

Builds on what you already know from Android from the foundation, not on an earlier puzzle here: you can start with this one.

The problem

In puzzle 2 you recorded a slow scroll. The profiler now shows a mountain of coloured bars. onBind() is wide, parseJson() inside it is wide, and format() appears three times in one chart and once, very wide, in another. Which bar is the one to fix?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

The call chart is a timeline. Each call is a bar from when it started to when it ended, and the functions it called, its callees, sit underneath it. If onBind() calls format() three times, you see three separate format() bars, one after another.

The flame chart takes the same recording and merges every call that has the same chain of callers into one bar. The three format() calls, all called from onBind(), become one bar as wide as the three together. Now width means "how much time in total", and left to right is no longer a timeline: the widest children are drawn first. That's why it's the fastest way to see where time goes.

Two numbers read the bars:

  • Total time: the whole bar, the function plus everything it called.
  • Self time: only the function's own code, the part of its bar not covered by children.

Start at the first caller's bar. (In Android Studio it's at the bottom: the flame chart is drawn upside down, callees stacked above their caller.) A wide bar whose child is just as wide is slow because of the child: follow the child. A bar noticeably wider than all its children together has self time: that's code to fix in that function.

The bottom-up view answers the opposite question: for a function that's slow everywhere, who calls it, and how much each caller spends.

The analogy

A call chart is your day in a calendar: every meeting at its time. A flame chart is the same week summarised by type: "meetings with Anna: 6 hours", one block, no times. You can't tell when, but you see at a glance where the week went.

Check yourself

In a flame chart, format() is drawn left of parseJson(). What does that tell you?

Right. Width is time; position isn't.

Not quite. A caller and its callees are stacked, not side by side.

Not quite. That's a call chart. In a flame chart the order is by width, not by when.

onBind() is 200 ms wide. Its only child, parseJson(), is 190 ms wide. Where's the time?

Right. Follow the child while it's as wide as the parent.

Not quite. Total time includes children; self time is only the gap they don't cover.

Not quite. Its width includes its child; only 10 ms is its own.

What's the difference between self time and total time?

Right. Own code vs own code plus callees.

Not quite. That's the two swapped. Re-read that part ↑

Sources
  • Android Studio: Flame chart ("identical methods or functions that share the same sequence of callers are collected and represented as one longer bar in a flame chart"; "the horizontal axis doesn't represent a timeline; instead, it indicates the relative amount of time each method or function takes to execute"; "the callees that consume the most CPU time appear first")
  • Android Studio: Top down and bottom up charts ("Self: the time the method or function call spent executing its own code and not that of its callees"; "Total: the sum of the method's Self and Children time"; "The Bottom Up tab displays a list of calls in which expanding a function or method's node displays its callers.")

What you now know

A call chart draws each call along a timeline, callees under their caller. A flame chart merges identical call stacks into one bar, so width means total time and left to right means nothing. A wide bar with a wide child is slow because of the child; a bar wider than all its children is slow in its own code: its self time.
